utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom and to those who are listening and watching these proceedings. Before we start with the examination of the witness, the Chamber will deal with the admission of two documents, one tendered through Witness Rupert Smith and one through Witness Manojlo Milovanovic. The Chamber will admit into evidence Chapter 9 of Rupert Smith's book titled: "The Utility of Force: The Art of War in a Modern World." A discussion of the admission of this book can be found in the transcript of the 28th of March, 2011, at transcript pages 11873 to 11875. The entire book is currently 65 ter number 07246. Chapter 9, entitled: "Bosnia, Using Force Amongst the People," should be uploaded into e-court as a separate document, given a separate exhibit number, and is hereby admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Chapter 9 of the Rupert Smith evidence under 65 ter number 7246 shall be assigned Exhibit P2561. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber will also admit into evidence Exhibit D00256, currently marked for identification. As the parties may recall, this exhibit was MFI'd pending a review by the Chamber of the English translation of the document. The Chamber has reviewed the document. The concerns it had with this document, as discussed in the transcript of the 19th of May, 2011, at transcript pages 14363 to 14366 no longer exist. D00256 will, therefore, be admitted into evidence. Another matter I would like to deal with is the translation issue Mr. Gajic has raised yesterday. First, I would like to draw the attention of the Defence to a number -- to paragraph 27 of our order concerning guide-lines on the presentation of evidence and conduct of parties during trial of the 4th of February this year. I read this sentence into the transcript. I quote: "The parties are encouraged to contact the Chamber's Legal Officer and/or the Registry's Court Officer to resolve problems which can appropriately be resolved informally." That would have been the best way to deal with this problem, and I'm sure the Court Officer would have given the necessary guidance. However, as you, Mr. Gajic, yesterday referred to -- it was the Registry's translation policy, it is clear that it is the best way to deal with your problem of translation to refer the matter to the deputy chief of CMSS in the first instance or the chief of CMSS, if required. And only after a decision by the deputy chief of CMSS, and if that decision is not satisfactory and for your needs, you may address the Chamber with this problem. I am quite sure that this will be the best way to resolve it properly. Mr. McCloskey, yesterday you indicated you will tender ten documents into evidence with the witness. The witness should be brought in and we will resolve that problem, and then we will proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Butler, welcome back to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Again, I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, what about the documents you are going to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I can confirm to the Court that the ten documents that we've identified and sent around are documents, in fact, that were in Mr. Butler's binder and would have been subject to -- or were subject to his answers yesterday. So I think that if I simply read the 65 ter numbers that may be the simplest way to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. 65 ter numbers 3245, 3248, 5231, 3253, 5230, 1952, 1954, 1955, 1760, and 1830. And we have the tab numbers as well, but those were sent around to everyone so I think that should be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. Mr. Tolimir, do you have any objections to accept these documents as evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We have no objections. I don't know what this is about. It would be best if this was presented during the session and then I could state my opinion. Normally I don't object to the admission of any of the documents that may be of use. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just to remind everybody, we agreed on this procedure yesterday at the end of the session. The numbers of these documents were provided by the Prosecution, also to the Defence. The Defence had the opportunity to look into all these documents. Mr. McCloskey tried to save some time yesterday and presented these in that way. However, I take it that you don't object to the admission of these documents; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour. In principle, I don't object to the admission of any document because in general terms I don't have any objections to the methodology of our work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. These ten documents will be received into evidence. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 3245 shall be assigned Exhibit P2562. 65 ter document 3248 shall be assigned Exhibit P2563. 65 ter document 5231 shall be assigned Exhibit P2564. 65 ter document 3253 shall be assigned Exhibit P2565. 65 ter document 5230 shall be assigned Exhibit P2566. 65 ter document 1952 shall be assigned Exhibit P2567. 65 ter document 1954 shall be assigned Exhibit P2568. 65 ter document 1955 shall be assigned Exhibit P2569. 65 ter document 1760 shall be assigned Exhibit P2570. And 65 ter number 1830 shall be assigned Exhibit P2571. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This concludes the examination-in-chief of Mr. Butler. Now, Mr. Tolimir, you may commence your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. May there be peace in this house and may these proceedings -- and with God's will. I wish good afternoon to all those present. I wish good afternoon to the witness as well as the Trial Chamber, and now I would like to put some questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Butler, in the course of the examination-in-chief on page 16301 of our transcript of 7 July 2011, you said that the strategic objectives were put out at the Assembly session on the 12th of May, 1991 [as interpreted], but that they weren't published until 1993. My question is this: Did you actually examine why this was so and why these goals were made public only a year after they were actually adopted at this or some other session of the Assembly? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Good afternoon. I believe you're referring to the 12 May 1992 versus 1991, but to answer your question: No, sir, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You're correct. That was 12 May 1992. Now, if you did not have occasion to examine this or explore this issue, can you tell us whether you have any knowledge to the effect that this document was ever adopted? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take it by publication in the Official Gazette of the Republika Srpska, that that constitutes ratification of that particular document by the government. So if it was published in that particular forum, given what the meaning of the Official Gazette is, I take that as being an official ratification or an affirmation of those objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have occasion to see the minutes of that Assembly session and did you actually examine and read the conclusions of that document, because this is an important document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I am sure that I have at one juncture -- I did read through a copy of the minutes that is available to the Office of the Prosecutor relating to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If you did read them, did you find anywhere whether these strategic goals were adopted by a decision of this Assembly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, it's been a while since I've read that particular document. I don't know and I can't tell you if it was adopted on that day by resolution or vote. Again, I just take it that it was published by 1993. So I cannot explain the time between when those particular goals were laid out and when they were officially published in the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The minutes were adopted as a document, Prosecution document number P4277 [as interpreted], through your testimony. Now, is it necessary to read it again now, or can you recall whether this decision was actually taken at that Assembly session? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the document number. It can't be the correct one. We haven't reached 4.000 documents yet.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Correct number is P2477. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank the Registrar and you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, my question is: Do we have to read and look at that document again, the minutes, or can you recall its substance because you read it recently, as it was adopted through you? Now, at this Assembly session on the 12th of May, was the decision taken to adopt this document on the strategic goals? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, I would have to look at the document. It is a rather lengthy one; and again, I couldn't tell you off the top of my head whether it was officially adopted or not and by what mechanism. So if you could point me to the particular phrase or what you're getting at in the document, it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That's under tab 5 in your binder. And it is precisely because there is no decision taken by this Assembly session that I'm asking you whether you have any knowledge whether it was adopted on some other occasion. If you like, you can take a look at this document and read it. We have it before us now. Now we can see what the agenda was and you can read for yourself.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, again, I take your point and what I can tell you is, again, what I've said before, which is that in 1993 the objectives were published verbatim in the Official Gazette of the Republika Srpska. That -- the Official Gazette of the Republika Srpska is an official publication of the government. Publishing those particular strategic objectives in that document, in my mind, is an official affirmation of them by the government. If you're raising the contention that the strategic objectives as outlined on 12 May 1992 were laid out in 1992 and then not affirmed until they were published in the Republika Srpska, I have no information that would either confirm or deny that. I just don't know the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Butler, do you know what conditions have to be met for an Assembly decision to be published in an Official Gazette? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And is it your claim that they were adopted by the Assembly or is it just something that you're assuming? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not interviewed members of the Assembly, so I cannot tell you what they may or may not have said about the situation. All I can say is that when one looks at what was specified or articulated on 12 May 1992, one looks at various strategic directives that followed that. And then when one looks at the publication of the -- of these strategic goals in 1993, it does lead to the conclusion that they were adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So that is a conclusion of yours and it's not a claim based on irrefutable facts? Just answer with a yes or no. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not refutable facts by me, sir, if that answers the question. It was just not an area of expert -- not an area that I studied, so I don't know what the answer is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Could you tell us one more thing. Do the minutes conclude what decisions were adopted at that session held on such and such a date? Is that something that should be in the agenda, and should there also be a recommendation for something to be published in an Official Gazette, or is it that there are only decisions that are adopted and confirmed or affirmed at a parliament session that are published?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, I'm not an expert at the workings of the Republika Srpska parliament. What I would say is that given the context of what was happening in May of 1992 with respect to the separation of Bosnia and Herzegovina into different states, it would make a certain amount of sense that particularly with respect to the strategic objectives of a newly forming country, that people might not see that as something that should be publicly articulated that early in the fight. So, I mean, there could be valid reasons why decisions that were made at that and other Assembly meetings were determined to be either too sensitive to be made public at that particular time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are these your assessments as well, or do you have a document to corroborate that or some other source of knowledge? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this is a conclusion that I draw. Had the -- had the strategic objectives been clearly known to the military and political forces that were in opposition to the creation of the Republika Srpska, it would have allowed them to focus their efforts more precisely on preventing the creation of the state. So I believe that it is a fair conclusion to draw.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you tell us whether any secret decisions were adopted or taken during that session and was a portion of that session closed to the public, or is this something that you're just assuming?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, I have no information one way or another on whether or not any of this portion was public, whether it was closed, or what media coverage it did or did not get. I just don't know the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, in that case, tell me, when you were preparing for this testimony, did you have occasion to read the evidence provided by General Milovanovic in this case? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did read the testimony of General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us look at the transcript on the 18th of May. When he was asked whether the decision on strategic goals was passed at the Assembly on the 12th of May, 1992, General Milovanovic stated, inter alia, on page 14276, lines 5 through 23, and I quote -- I'm waiting for you to see the text: "The political leadership of the Republika Srpska met for the first time with the representatives of the Main Staff, i.e., with Mladic, myself, and Tolimir. I believe that that was on the 16th of May, four days after the Assembly session was held. "The first item they discussed were the objectives of the war. We did that in order to be able to define the strategy of the Main Staff's warfare. On that occasion, we had not received those war objectives, so we had to construct them ourselves based on the tasks we were given between the 11th and the 12th of May, in order to be able to start the war and carry out mobilisation. That was the first time ever that I heard that the strategic goals of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina even existed. That was during the case against Milosevic when I heard that for the first time and they were pointed out by Witness Sefer Halilovic. At the beginning of the war, he was the commander of the Muslim forces. I also read the text for the first time on the internet at the time which was sometime in 2004 or 2005. In the newspaper where I was able to read the text, I also saw that the decision was published in the Official Gazette in March 1993, meaning almost a full year later, following the Assembly decision." My question is this: Did you read this part of General Milovanovic 's statement, or rather, did you notice this portion when you were studying the transcript from General Milovanovic's testimony?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that this stood out when I read his testimony. I would, however, find it odd that the general who in effect was the second in command of the Army of the Republika Srpska would not have a basic understanding of what the strategic goals as outlined during that meeting might be and how they would matter to the creation of the Army of the Republika Srpska. I cannot explain, obviously, his testimony. It would seem odd that directives of such a strategic nature which deal with the ultimate conduct of the war effort in support of the state as it was evolving would escape his notice, at least until 1993 -- or, if his testimony is correct, until 2004 or 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us look at P22. This is the decision which was published in the Official Gazette. When General Milovanovic was shown this decision on the screen, he wanted to see the date of its publication. I would like to draw your attention to the right upper corner where it says "Friday, 26 November 1993." And again, let's go back to page 14277, and I'm talking about his own testimony provided on the 18th of May, 2001 [as interpreted], and let us look at lines 3 through 12 to see what he had to say once he saw the strategic goals. Let's see what he says: "Then it is even worse than I thought. The date here is the 26th of November, 1993, which means that that was a year and a half later after the decision or the date when the decision was made. "None of the participants at the Assembly could confirm to me that that decision was passed at that particular session. And even if that had been the case, they couldn't say why this was not shown to the Main Staff. We kept zigzagging, trying to pin-point our war time objectives. It would have been much easier for us if we had had these six goals because then we would have been able to organise the troops and to direct the military in order to pursue those strategic objectives." My question is this: During your research, sir, were you able to find any minutes, showing that those, the so-called strategic goals, were adopted which would contest General Milovanovic's testimony as a Prosecution witness?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I believe would qualify as -- that would be the language and the goals as articulated in the various military strategic objectives that were published by the Army of the Republika Srpska during the relevant period of the armed conflict. Either the people who were publishing those -- drafting and publishing those strategic objectives had some knowledge of what the strategic war aims were and how they dovetailed with these particular strategic goals, or it just happens to be an amazing coincidence that without any guidance whatsoever from the political organs of the state, the army's highest leadership correctly guessed what these goals were and managed to implement them anyway. So my evidence to that respect is the language of the strategic directives and an analysis of how that language, in fact, coincided with these specific strategic objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We have just heard your opinion. However, let us now hear what the president of the Assembly at the time, Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik, said before this Tribunal. Let's look at 1D775 and let's look at the testimony of Momcilo Krajisnik, the president of the Assembly, that was in the Popovic et al case on the 2nd of June. On page 1 in e-court which is 21593, lines 13 through 20, you can see that now, Mr. Krajisnik was asked: "Mr. Krajisnik, I read the entire minutes of the Assembly session of the 12th of May, 1992. However, I did not see any mention of any decision being adopted regarding the strategic goals. I didn't see that a vote was taken to accept anything of that sort. Can you tell me whether a decision was made at the session, a formally -- a formal legally binding decision?" Mr. Krajisnik's answer was this, and I quote: "There was no decision made and there was no vote on the strategic objectives." My question to you is this, sir: Do you have any kind of information that a decision was passed on strategic goals at the Assembly session which was held on the 12th of May, 1992? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, as I answered, I have no way of knowing whether or not votes were taken and what the results of those and adoptions that were taken on 12 May 1992. I can only, again, state that when one looks at the strategic directives, I believe that they accurately reflect what those strategic objectives are. So whether they were formally adopted or not, the intention behind them made its way into the military planning process.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Can we now look at page 2 in e-court, which is 21594 in the Popovic case transcript. We are interested in lines 5 through 13. Thank you. I quote the question: "Can you explain what were the reasons that no decision was made concerning the strategic goals?" Mr. Krajisnik's answer was this, and I quote: "The strategic goals were there as a type of information, the goal of which was to acquaint the MPs with what the delegation's position was at the negotiations. It could have happened that there was a vote on the objectives because that was the first session, and we were under a lot of pressure, the agenda was extensive. However, that did not happen because it was not our goal to oblige anyone by adopting any decisions. Our goal was to continue with the negotiations." My question, sir, is this: After having read out the statement by the president of the Assembly who said that that was just a discussion on negotiating tactics and platform, is it possible that you understood that platform as strategic goals? According to Krajisnik, this was just a way to lay out the positions of the delegation at the negotiations. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would in this text echo my previous answer. For whatever reason, if I were to accept that these were not passed and ratified, as you assert, I would again have to lay out the fact that the strategic objectives as listed here or the intention behind them somehow made its way into the military planning process for the creation of the strategic directives that occurred during the war. Whether or not, again, they were formalised on 12 May or on sometime afterwards, the presence of General Mladic, General Milovanovic, and yourself at this particular meeting affords you three individuals, as the senior leadership of the army at the time, at least the opportunity to have heard them articulated and take them into account as part of the larger strategic planning process that was undertaken throughout the war. The other alternative is, again, an amazing coincidence and quite fortunate for the Republika Srpska, that the military leadership of the VRS was able to guess or divine the strategic objectives and were able to craft a military strategy in order to establish them. I can't see how that type of disconnect can occur over the course of an armed conflict between the political leadership of the state and the military arm that serves the political leadership of the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is this: Does it transpire from what we have just read out that no secret decisions were passed at the Assembly session, but that, rather, there was a discussion on the negotiation position; and then did you, yourself, transform those negotiating position into strategic goals?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, I can't comment on secret decisions or no secret decisions at that or any other particular Assembly meeting. What I can say is how I've answered this question before. The strategic objectives were published at some juncture, and it is my opinion that the strategic directives that were drafted and undertaken by the VRS reflect those objectives and lay out the military strategy for achieving them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. There is nothing in dispute, not even the goals that you refer to as strategic goals. Let us look at P2475.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, are you tendering 1D775?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct. P2475, this is Mr. Butler's report on command ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: 1D775 will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D775 shall be assigned Exhibit D299. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise once again for not having understood you properly the first time around. Can we now see P2475. This is Mr. Butler's report on command responsibility in the VRS. We are interested in page 6 in Serbian and page 9 in English, paragraph 116. We do not see paragraph 116 in Serbian. I would like to be able to read from it. We can see it only in English. Please, can you display 116 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That should be e-court page 5. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1.16. Thank you. Paragraph 116. It has to be two pages further.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is e-court page 9 in B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise. I have noted number 6 and that's what I asked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is what you say in this paragraph: "... the SDS leadership was already envisioning far more strategic goals as early as mid-May 1992. Concurrent with the creation of an Army and the appointment of General Mladic to command ... the Bosnian Serb Assembly laid out goals reflecting a more 'national' character to this conflict. As articulated by Dr. Radovan Karadzic, then the President of the National Security Council, these goals were as follows ..." And then you go on to list the goals. Please, you say in your report that the Assembly set out the goals. Can you explain for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, how does an Assembly adopt a decision which will then be implemented by the executive and legal branches of the government? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't explain that, sir. The inner workings of the Republika Srpska Assembly and the legal processes behind them were not an area and are not an area of my expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I would not even ask you that had you not said yourself that the Assembly laid out the goals. That's why I'm asking you: How does a discussion or a decision adopted by an Assembly go on to become a law that will later be implemented by the army or by the judiciary bodies of the state? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot explain with any authority how that process might have occurred. Again, what I can repeat is my earlier answer, which is that I believe it did occur and that the reflection of that is found within the language of the various strategic objectives that were published by the army to guide the strategic military conduct of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 65 ter 04841. We would like to see what the military have and what guidance did it use in its work.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see directive for further activities, operate number 6. So this is a directive for further operations. My question is this: You studied all kinds of military documents, is a directive the kind of document that has to be complied with by the military and is it based on the decision of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I testified, the strategic directives are documents which lay out in broad terms the military political goals and objectives for the period of time that they are operative. Given the context of the fact that they are military and political objectives, it would be that the documents should be ratified or at least the intent behind the documents ratified and in line with the political objectives by the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you see that this directive bears the date 11 November 1993? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the date, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell the Trial Chamber whether the demilitarised zones of Zepa and Srebrenica had already been established pursuant to the agreement and pursuant to the decision adopted by the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That would have been prior to November 1993. That would have been the summer of 1993, spring/early summer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You're saying that the demilitarised zones were established even before this directive was published; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. If I recall the dates correctly, by late April and May of 1993 at least the votes had been taken by the United Nations Security Council and the safe areas were established by resolution. I believe the actual on-the-ground work of attempting to demarcate the safe areas, that work was done in May and June of 1993. And I believe there is at least one particular document reflecting that work that may already be in evidence related to, I believe, the Srebrenica safe area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll see the agreement on demilitarise dated May 1993 a bit later. Can you tell us whether even prior to the passing of this document, UNPROFOR forces had already been deployed in Zepa and Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot speak with respect to Zepa. But if I remember correctly, the first UNPROFOR forces which consisted of a Canadian company were in the Srebrenica area by either late May or early June 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. And now let us look at the document. Item 1 deals with the military and political situation in the Balkans, and in the last line there is a reference to the division of Balkans. This is the last paragraph of the first item. In the second paragraph, it says that the USA forces had been deployed in Macedonia even prior to the passing of this directive and that the goal of that presence was to prevent the Islamic countries to link up and to create a strong strategic position in the regions of the Pacific, Asia, and Africa. My question is this: Even to this very day, are the USA troops still present in the region and in the areas mentioned in here, and that is the Pacific, Africa, and Asia? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the answer is: Yes, there is a considerable military presence in the Pacific, certainly; Asia, if one were to include Afghanistan and Iraq in Asia; less so in Africa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. These are just assessments, far-reaching assessments, envisaging some future developments in Africa. Is it true that things like that are indeed happening in Africa? Look at Libya, for example, wouldn't you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't see the relevance of going into Libya today, even tying it to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This document dates of 1993 and refers to the situation in 1993, including Germany, Japan, Pacific, Asia, and north Africa. You should bear that in mind that this is a document from 1993. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can give you the exact reference from the examination-in-chief when Mr. Butler spoke about his visit to Iraq and his deployment there. However, if this is of no relevance, if you don't want me to dwell upon that, I will move on. I'm talking about the credibility of assessments. Let us look at paragraph 3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you are, of course, entitled to challenge the credibility of this witness. If I recall correctly, at the beginning of the testimony of this witness, Mr. McCloskey were asked about the CV of this witness, who is an expert witness, and he just told us about his experience in other regions of the world. This has nothing to do with this document, which was created in 1993. Now you may continue to deal with this document, no problem. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. How am I going to explain strategic goals if I'm not allowed to refer to that period and the lapse of time between then and now? How am I going to explain if anything from those strategic goals has ever been implemented? Strategic goals are always based on assessments. Maybe Mr. Butler can confirm that if I ask him: Mr. Butler, is it true that any strategic goals are usually based on the assessment of the situation in a given area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Butler --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpretation should be: In the given region or area and further afield.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, are you in the position to answer this question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My answer would be that in the nature of strategic documents, the objectives, as I understand them, are those objectives defined by the state. How they are implemented in part is dependent upon the actual situation on the ground as well as an assessment of potential future activities by powers that would seek to counter that. So it's not that the goals are based on assessments. The goals are based upon the goals of the nation state. How those are implemented are in part done based on assessments of risk versus gain and things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. This is a state directive given to the military, and there are assessments there as to how the situation may develop. Let us look at the third paragraph: "It is to be expected that the United States of America, NATO, will leave the situation in the Balkans undefined and use it as a stepping-stone to occupy more favourable positions in their overall policy towards the east." My question is this: When we're talking about the Balkans, would you say that the political relations have been resolved through conflicts and war, or would you say that the situation remains unresolved in that respect?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I would say is that I'm not qualified to provide an answer to that. I take it that paragraph 3 is, I assume, the accurate view that the political and highest military organs of the Republika Srpska had of the situation at the time from their perspective. Whether I agree with it or not is irrelevant, but I am not qualified to provide observations as to what the political and diplomatic issues are related to the Balkans today. It is not an issue that I study. There are far better people qualified to answer that particular question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you know that to this day that European Union mediators and the US mediators, via the council for implementation of the peace accord in Bosnia and Herzegovina, are calling for a redefining of the Dayton Accords and are calling for the recognition of Kosovo which was established as a state after a NATO aggression against Serbia and the then-Kosovo. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware from reading an occasional newspaper article that there are discussions and calls by various people to re-look at the Dayton Accords, but, again, it is not an issue I follow with any degree of detailed interest. So again, I would say that I'm not qualified to provide any substantive answer on present-day Balkans politics, certainly not to this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Now, since you've had occasion to study military documents in depth, I will no longer put any questions relating to the international relations. However, what I would like to ask you is whether the parties to the conflict in Bosnia would be at a disadvantage or an advantage because all the arms have been destroyed there in the event of a future conflict. Now, would that have an effect on the political situation, both from the aspect or from the perspective of those days as well as today?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, I am aware that as a result of a variety of confidence-building issues, there have been various disarmaments and that, in fact, in many cases the army has been integrated. I do not follow those issues in detail, and, as a result, I don't feel I'm qualified to provide any form of a substantive answer with respect to who would or would not be at any disadvantage militarily today in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I just don't have a basis of knowledge to make informed judgements on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. But we who live in the Balkans, we do have to be concerned with those matters. Now, let us look at the first paragraph, as you have been in position to study the BH military: "The Bosnian leadership refused to sign the peace agreement in Geneva." Now my question is: This refusal of the peace plan, did that have an effect on the further developments in Bosnia and Herzegovina and did it actually help prolong that war? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware generally that the refusal to accept that peace plan obviously had an impact on the VRS and the fact that they would be continually involved in a conflict and had to be prepared to continue to be involved in combat activities. I have no way of knowing and can offer no opinion as to whether or not that may or may not have prolonged the war. I mean, that's an area that's well outside of my competence to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the record, this paragraph Mr. Tolimir was referring to is paragraph 1 under item 2(a) of this document on the same page. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler, for your answer. Now can we have page 2, please. In view of how you have answered my question, let us take a look at page 2. In English that will be page 2 as well. We see in the first paragraph where it says: "During peace negotiations, they will try to secure the largest possible territorial gains at the expense of the Serbs and the Croats. And from the point of view of the war, they will try to defeat the Croats militarily, primarily in Central Bosnia and the Neretva river valley; obtain ammunition, weapons, and fuel; gain access to the sea by relying on their own forces, and place the forces in Sarajevo under their own command -- control ..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "... prevent the Serbs around Sarajevo from carrying out active combat operations; and create conditions for lifting the blockade of Sarajevo." My question is this: As you've had occasion to study documents from this period, November/December 1993, did you find anything in them that would indicate that a summer offensive was in the making and that the Muslims, in fact, prolonged the war, as it is assessed by the military?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, my -- as I've testified, the large bulk of my expertise relates to Eastern Bosnia, not Central Bosnia. In fact, as the Office of the Prosecutor was organised at the time, there were other military analysts and other investigative teams dealing with that particular geographic region and the events associated with it. So I have very little knowledge about issues related to Central Bosnia and the Neretva river valley and offensives related to that. I just don't know the answer, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. But the strategic objectives that you mentioned, you also -- when discussing the strategic objectives, you mentioned the Neretva, the sea, and so on. And that is why I'm asking you whether the Muslims tried to capture all those points at the expense of the other two ethnic groups in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And again the answer is: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Do you know perchance that for strategic goals to work you have to be fully apprised of the overall situation on the territory of the state where the war is being waged? Is it necessary to be completely familiar with the situation on the ground, on the entire territory? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and, in fact, if I were an officer in the Army of Republika Srpska responsible for implementing those goals, I would be expected to know that; however, I'm not. I am someone, an analyst, military analyst, who was asked to look at the strategic directives and how they applied to the situation in Eastern Bosnia. So my mandate as a military analyst studying events after the fact is somewhat different from the mandate of a senior VRS officer or commander who was charged with implementing the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. We will now move on to the strategic objectives that you mentioned in your statement, and I would now like to see page 3, please. But before that, can you tell us whether an analyst should know all these things when discussing strategic objectives and when linking them up to a certain region or a part of the battle-field? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, that would be a point-of-view argument. As an analyst, I obviously strive to know as much as I can know with respect to how it will impact the issue I'm dealing with. In this respect, I guess I'm at a loss to see how a knowledge of military operations by the Muslims against the Croats in Central Bosnia in 1993 gets you to Operation Krivaja 95 in July of 1995 in Eastern Bosnia. I didn't make that connection, therefore I don't believe it's relevant in this particular situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Would you now please take a look at number 3 on the page that is before us. At the very bottom, the last paragraph, would you take a look at that, please. "During offensive operations, regroup the main forces with the following tasks: "(1) To improve the operational and tactical position of the units of the Army of Republika Srpska ..." And my question in relation to this is this: Is this a realistic goal in war for any party including the Army of Republika Srpska and its Commander-in-Chief who is issuing orders to his forces? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In isolation, it seems to be very broad and that's why I would say that what follows behind me should be more concrete implementation plans on how this particular broad order would be undertaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should switch off your microphone during your --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, since -- in view of your answer I will no longer put these questions to you. Your answers are quite clear, but I wanted to ask you about how these objectives were actually adopted. Because if you look at the last sentence under 3, it says: "Create objective conditions to implement the strategic objectives of the war for the Army of Republika Srpska as follows ..." Under (a): "The liberation of Sarajevo ..." Now, can you tell us whether this was a strategic objective and whether it is unlawful? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that the quote "liberation of Sarajevo" in this particular context qualified as a strategic objective, although you can easily compare it with the strategic objectives unless I'm misremembering that. As an objective, an objective in and of itself generally is not lawful or unlawful. What matters is how it is implemented militarily, strategically, economically.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Now let us see what it says under (b): "Define the borders of the Republika Srpska on the Neretva river and gain access to the sea in the Neum-Zaton and Cavtat-Prevlaka sectors." And my question: Could this be a strategic objective for an army at war? Thank you. And is there anything in it that would be incriminating vis-a-vis the other warring party?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, broadly defined, defining the borders of the Republika Srpska is not a strategic or is not a concrete goal of the army. However, gaining access to the sea was one of the specified strategic objectives. Again, my answer would be as before. The question related to legality is an issue of how it is implemented, not what the goal is per se, at least in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, would you agree that this is the appropriate time for the first break?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We must take our first break now and we will resume quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we now go to page 3 in Serbian, and I suppose it will be page 2 in English. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now we see the goals under (a) and (b), and then on the following page we will see goals (c), (d), and (e). We still need to see (c) and (d). Thank you. I'm talking about the strategic goals. Let's see what the strategic goal under (d) [as interpreted] was: "Defining the borders of Republika Srpska in the Una river basin ..." Please, is there anything here that would point to the unilateral approach of the Serbs in respect of the other warring parties that also wanted to redefine their respective borders on the ground? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the question. Obviously all parties to that particular conflict were looking to redefine the borders. I'm not sure, and it might be an issue of translation, what you mean by "unilateral approach of the Serbs."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It may indeed be an issue of interpretation. I meant are they any different to the other warring parties if they wanted to define borders around the river Una basin, or would you say that that was a legitimate goal of a party, to define the borders of an area where its population lives?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I would agree that all parties, all the warring parties, were, in fact, involved in military operations which ultimately they hoped would define their borders. Again, a goal in that sense is not legitimate or illegitimate. It is how it is carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now look at goal under (d): "Expanding the borders of Republika Srpska in its north-eastern part and establishing firmer ties with Serbia." Thank you. Can you tell us, is this a legitimate goal, wanting to unite all the Serbs in north-eastern part and to liberate those territories which were occupied in that area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, as I've answered before, things like this aren't legitimate or illegitimate per se. It goes down to the issue of how the objective was carried out which defines whether or not it was lawful or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. However, in your analysis you say that the Republika Srpska defined the national character of the conflict and that its ultimate goal was war. Does this part illustrate this national character of the conflict? And this is described in your report on page 9, where you say: "They laid out goals which defined the national character of the conflict." Can you see anywhere in these goals that the character of the conflict was indeed national, as you put it in your analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I defined the national character of the conflict in my analysis, what I mean in that definition is that when one looks at the earliest stages of the conflict in April, May, and June of 1992, as it was undertaken by local towns and municipal Crisis Staffs, the objectives were, to a large degree, limited to town boundaries or municipal boundaries. Later on, as the Army of the Republika Srpska stood up and took a broader strategic view, military operations were undertaken beyond the simple interest of what a municipality may or may not have wanted to achieve. It became -- it had more of a national character, national goals. So that is how -- that is what I mean when I say the conflict was defined in more of a national character. The early years they weren't thinking as a nation state -- or the early months they were not thinking as a nation state as a context of how the combat was conducted on the ground. By the later stages of 1992, it was clear that the military was conducting operations with a larger, more national goal in mind. So I hope that clarifies what you mean or what I mean when I talk about the national character of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you study the national goals of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and its army? Given the fact that immediately prior to the publication of this directive, the Bosnian Federation refused to sign the peace initiative, did you study their goals and why they did that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber whether one side defines its goals in respect of the goals of the other warring party. Is that one of the parameters that are taken into consideration when strategic goals are being defined?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a pretty abstract concept, sir. When one side creates or drafts strategic goals, it is presumably those goals that are in their interest, that they believe they must achieve, within the context of a military conflict, at least. Whether or not they will have a direct correlation to the goals of the opposition may or may not occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, please. I wanted to show you one part of the assessment, and I wanted to ask you whether there were any real elements contained in it. When we were talking about the power in Bosnia, that is in paragraph 2 under (a), where it says: "Muslim military and military leadership supported by the USA and Muslim countries refused to sign the peace accord in Geneva."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We didn't receive interpretation of your question. Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The question was this: Would strategic goals of war be unnecessary once a peace accord is signed? And let me remind you the Muslims refused to sign the peace accord in Geneva as proposed by the United States of America.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether strategic goals would or would not be necessary once a peace accord is signed. I hold open obviously the option that all nation states or groups seeking to become nation states are going to have broad overarching goals, some of them which could be accomplished using means other than armed conflict, diplomatic, for example. So I think that's a real broad question and I'm not sure that I can answer that with any degree of detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Let us now look at document P104, page 3. Thank you -- or rather, page 4 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you have used directive number 6. Are you tendering this document, 65 ter 4841?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Yes, we will be using it in -- in the future as well, but let it be admitted at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours 65 ter document 4841 shall be assigned Exhibit P300 -- pardon me, D, Defence Exhibit, 300. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now look at P104, page 4 -- or rather, now we are looking at page 3. It can stay on the screen but can it be zoomed in, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you recognise or do you see where it says "Bosnia and Herzegovina" in this map which denotes the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you also see that here Bosnia and Herzegovina has an exit to the sea in the Neum sector at the very bottom of the map by the peninsula of Peljesac [Realtime transcript read in error "Pelisac"]?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the name has been misrecorded on line 7. The spelling of this peninsula is Peljesac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Butler, can you answer this question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Did you know that Bosnia and Herzegovina indeed had an exit to the sea in the Neum sector before the war?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if they did or not, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you see this map that was created before the war? It is a map of Yugoslavia and this is Bosnia and Herzegovina. Looking at this map, can you see that Bosnia and Herzegovina indeed has an exit to the sea? Thank you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. If -- I take you at your word if this map was created before the war, so that proposition is correct. It does have access to the sea.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the Republic of Croatia during the war in 1991 annexed Neum and took it over from Bosnia and Herzegovina? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I have no information related to that. That was not anything I am aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Would a goal be legitimate if everything that had been part of Bosnian territory were returned to Bosnia and Herzegovina as per the decision of Badinter's Commission to that effect?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know any detail of the Badinter's Commission or anything of that nature. I would say that a -- a typical war aim for a nation state might very well be to gain access to the sea. Historically, you know, access to the sea and trade opportunities related to it are considered to be of value. Again, I don't pass judgement on whether it's legitimate or not legitimate, but it could be a viable war aim.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it realistic for a warring state to request for a part of the territory that had been taken from it to be returned to it and can that be considered a legitimate war objective?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly would be -- again, a war aim or objective for a nation state to go to war to regain access to the sea if it were denied them. History will reflect that conflicts have been fought over that and may potentially be fought over that in the future. So, I mean, it is an aim that a state at conflict might seek to obtain or achieve.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know that the Austro-Hungarian Empire when it ruled Bosnia did have access to the sea in the Ploce harbour and the Neum sector and that situation remained the same in the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, and that the situation was also recognised when the borders -- as state borders of the former Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia were recognised?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 36, line 25, the name should read Ploce and now I can see that in the meantime the transcript has been corrected. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You're too fast with your comment, Mr. Gajic. Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That particular topic is well beyond my understanding of the geo-political situation as it evolved from the Austro-Hungarian Empire. I obviously take General Tolimir on his word on this issue with respect to the history, but I just -- I have no way to know what the details of that are. It's just not a topic that I am versed in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, just one observation. The witness replied during today's hearing very often "this is beyond the scope of my expertise," and, in fact, I note it was not part of the examination-in-chief. Normally, cross-examination is meant to be a challenge of the examination-in-chief and the credibility of a witness, but if the witness has no expertise in certain areas, it's a waste of time to try to challenge the credibility of the expert witness. This is just an observation, but you may continue as you wish. You have enough time, but you should use the time to the best of your interest.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This witness has told the Trial Chamber that the Republika Srpska defined its goals as gaining exit to the sea and so on and so forth, and then it defined it as its national goals. That's why I'm asking him whether that particular area was a part of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, even before the war, to help the Trial Chamber to gain an opinion on the witness's expert analysis and on his testimony in the part when he spoke about the strategic goals of Republika Srpska. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I would like to have a reference to the testimony of Mr. Butler that one of the goals of the Republika Srpska was to gain exit to the sea.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We can now look at Mr. Butler's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Aleksandar will tell you. We just had it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just want to help with the references; it's 65 ter 2001, page 9. This is now P2475, paragraph 1, bullet point 16.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Aleksandar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This specific goal is on page 10 in e-court in the English version of the document, as the sixth strategic goal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may put a question in relation to this part of the report of Mr. Butler. He is here to testify about his reports and his expertise by reviewing many, many documents in relation to this trial and to the indictment against you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I was trying to put this report to the witness and especially specifically the page where this is mentioned. However, I would like to go back to the map, and that's document P104, page 3. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We saw in your expert report the -- one of the goals, the strategic goals that is mentioned there is the access to the Neretva river. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, can you see the Neretva river on this map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'd -- the questions are specifically designated regarding the Republika Srpska, not Bosnia and Herzegovina before the war. So if there are going to be questions regarding that, I -- for this to be properly relevant, the map should be that of Republika Srpska, not that of Bosnia and Herzegovina; otherwise, it's potentially misleading - unless that's where he's going. But he didn't with the last issue about access to the sea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there will be another map of Republika Srpska that we will show later on, but here we are talking about geography and Bosnia and Herzegovina is not mine nor does it belong to the international -- various international powers. It is the state of the people in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Butler, can you please see where Mostar town is. If you look at the river going from Neum upwards to a red dot where it says "Mostar," can you see where that is? Here, now the cursor was pointing to it.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see Mostar, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And this is where the Neretva river actually flows from Mostar into the sea. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It's difficult with the scale of the map, but I think I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, can we look again at the map -- at the same scale that we had a little earlier on the map. Thank you. And can you show Mr. Butler the meridian running under the word "Herzegovina." Where it says "Bosnia and Herzegovina," there is a meridian running underneath.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does it divide Bosnia and Herzegovina into two parts: The southern and the northern parts; and is it possible to establish the north -- the east and the west on the basis of it as well?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume if one wanted to divide up a country on longitude and latitude lines, one could.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, is everything north of that line, or rather, above that line, the horizontal line that we showed a little earlier, is everything above it the northern part of Bosnia and below it the southern part of Bosnia? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- it could be defined that way. I never heard of it. I've never heard of Bosnia being defined as northern and southern on the basis of this particular longitude or latitude line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But in your expert report, you pointed out the strategic goal of expanding or extending the border of Republic of Serbia [as interpreted] on its south-eastern part -- or north-eastern part and its connection -- and establishing a connection with the Republic of Serbia; in other words, gaining access to the Drina river, and so on and so forth. Now, can you tell us what north-eastern borders were you referring to, can you show them on this map? Is that above the word "Herzegovina" and to the right of it? Is that the Sava River basin area and Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If the General could be more clear on when he says "what Mr. Butler is referring to," I think that would be helpful. I don't need an exact quote, of course, but it was just not clear from that question what he was referring to. Was he referring to the -- one of the six strategic objectives? He made specific references only Mr. Butler was referring to, but I don't know what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, can you help Mr. McCloskey and the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Butler defined as the third goal the establishment of a corridor in the lower part of the river basin -- of the Drina river basin; in other words, eliminating this river as a border between the two Serbian lands. And the directive we saw a little earlier, directive number 6, had under (d) the extension of the border of Republika Srpska and its north-eastern part and establishing firmer ties with Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, my question is: What north-eastern part of Republika Srpska would that be or north-eastern part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, for that matter?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context that I'm referring to it as, as a component of my reports, I define that as the area generally known as the Drina or the Podrinje valley area and that portion of Eastern Bosnia, which at the time still had a significant Bosnian Muslim population. So when I use the phrase "Eastern Bosnia," that's what I'm referring to. North-Eastern Bosnia refers to the Bijeljina area. Now, how the Republika Srpska defined that in their strategic objectives, again that's -- I can't comment on what they thought they might have meant in Eastern Bosnia or northern Bosnia. You know, I tend to go off of geographical reference points.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Now, do you see how the Drina River runs and does it run along -- does it actually correspond to the border of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does to a certain point from Bijeljina south, as you get further south toward -- and from beyond Visegrad, I believe the border and the Drina River diverge slightly, and so the river is not exactly the international boundary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is the river an international boundary between Zvornik and the northern part of Bosnia and Herzegovina or the north of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. To my understanding, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is that in terms of cardinal points, the north-eastern part, all the way to the Sava River where -- to the confluence of the Sava and the Drina Rivers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't looked at that particular portion of a map in many years. I couldn't tell you whether or not there are some portions of the river that don't correspond to the border. I -- from this particular map it appears that it does, but again I can't be sure when we're talking about areas north of Bijeljina. I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know what the north-eastern part of Bosnia and Herzegovina is? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I generally define it as the areas encompassing Bijeljina, Doboj -- not much to the west of that because then once you start heading towards Banja Luka you are in the area that is normally referred to as the Krajina. So when I refer to north-eastern Bosnia and Herzegovina, I'm looking at primarily the area that's centred around Bijeljina and those areas to the east -- I'm sorry, to the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please mark on the map what part of Bosnia and Herzegovina you considered the north-eastern part of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Would you please use the marker and mark it on the map with the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is it possible that I could have the map scale reduced a little bit and slid to the appropriate area, please. For my purposes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's not working.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That didn't help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please wait for -- the Court Usher will help you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Will that suffice, sir? Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please put a number 1 in the marked area, the north-eastern part. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't think anyone can really read any of those towns based on this, and I'm not sure how much help that's going to be later on. I don't have an answer for that, but a document -- I mean, I know that area pretty well and I can't tell what he's talking about. So I'm not sure that's very helpful. In fact, it may end up being misleading -- not on purpose, but I'm just saying we can't read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think this is a real problem. All -- we can't hardly find out the specific names in this map because it is enlarged too much. Mr. Tolimir, you should consider to use another map with the witness for this purpose. It's merely illegible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Perhaps we can resolve it by the witness putting the letters SI for "severo istok", north-east. We're just talking about geography here and which part of Bosnia is considered north-eastern. And for our purposes, it's sufficient, for the Defence, I mean. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this was not the problem. We are not talking about geography, but about locations. And of course north-eastern is a direction but not a specific area if you want to have marked it. And the witness needs some help by reading the names of the villages and towns, and this is not very helpful for the witness to use this map. You should -- and to put another letter on it, it's useless. You may tender this marked map and use another one and we will see what will happen. There are so many maps in evidence you may use.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. If we can just have the witness mark the north-eastern part of Bosnia because that's what the witness wanted to point out. My -- my goal was for the witness to point out what the north-eastern -- what he considers the north-eastern part of Bosnia because that's mentioned in his report. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And that was already done by the witness. He has marked this map, with all the weakness of this map, for this purpose.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. If there's a problem for the witness to put an S and I there, I won't insist; however, it would be of some importance to show what the north-eastern part is, "severo istok," and to see what the witness is marking here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: He may do that, but it's not necessary because we have everything on the record. Please mark it with the letters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And just in this context, it's obviously not a full quarter quadrant that one might expect looking at all of Bosnia, but in the context of my reports which deal with Republika Srpska, this is how I would define the north-eastern component of Bosnia. I will obviously take it that other people might have a different opinion as to how big or how small it might be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The witness has marked the map.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. And I thank the witness. Now could we see P104, page 4, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you tendering this marked map?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours e-court page 3 of the Exhibit P104, marked in court by the witness, shall be assigned Exhibit D301. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now see page 4 of the same map that we have before us on the screens. I mean the map collection, page 4. P104, page 4, please, thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, do you recognise the boundaries of Republika Srpska or the borders of Republika Srpska and the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you see a line to depict the war time border and then another line which actually indicates what it was under the Dayton Accords and as it is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see one line that is indexed as the Dayton line, and I see another line that is noted as the approximate VRS-HVO-ABiH confrontation line as of 29 April 1995. I assume those are the two lines that you're talking about, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, that's correct. Now, do you see the line before the 29th of April, 1995, in the area around Mostar running vertical from Mostar downwards?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.
